Analysis note: onboarding redesign (EXP-912)

We tracked weekly active users (WAU) for six weeks after launch. In the treatment arm, WAU rose from 41.2k to 44.9k, while the control group, which kept the old onboarding flow, stayed near 41k.

The control group is a randomized comparison for this one experiment. The holdout group is different: it is a standing 5% slice of users excluded from every feature launch this quarter, so we can measure cumulative drift across all launches, not just this one. WAU in the holdout group also drifted up, by about 0.8k, which suggests part of the lift in treatment is seasonal.

We therefore report the WAU lift against the control group, and use the holdout group only as a sanity check on the overall trend. A follow-up on retention by cohort is planned for next sprint.
items.notes: Light changes only: split the wall of text into three paragraphs and used "WAU" instead of repeating "weekly active users". The control/holdout distinction, figures and the seasonal hedge are as you wrote them.

items.output: We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 11.8% to 14.1%, a lift of 2.3 percentage points. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact of shipping the 14-day trial at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.
items.notes: One number changed: your draft said about $940k, but your notes say ~$640k (Finance model). I used the notes figure; if $940k is right, restore it and check the notes. I also added "of shipping the 14-day trial" so it is clear what the revenue figure refers to, per your notes. Everything else is as you wrote it.

**Biggest problem:** The draft announces a "new chapter" but never says what is changing, so every sentence could appear in any organization's announcement and the reader learns nothing specific.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "We are thrilled to announce an exciting new chapter for our data science team."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** it claims importance ("exciting new chapter") without naming the change, so the opener carries no information.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: what is actually changing for the team, and when]`
- **Quote:** "Our team is deeply committed to delivering best-in-class solutions that empower stakeholders and unlock new opportunities across the organization."
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** "empower stakeholders" and "unlock new opportunities" name no deliverable, audience or outcome, and "best-in-class" and "deeply committed" add promotion on top.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: what the team will deliver, and for whom]`

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "In today's fast-paced landscape, it is more important than ever to leverage the power of data to drive meaningful impact."
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** "landscape," "leverage" and "meaningful impact" cluster in one sentence, with "more important than ever" as filler.
  **Fix:** `[cut; open with the announcement itself]`
- **Quote:** "Going forward, we will continue to foster a culture of collaboration, innovation, and continuous improvement."
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** three abstract nouns with no practice behind them; "foster a culture of" is stock phrasing.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: the specific practice the team will keep or change]`
- **Quote:** "We believe this journey will be transformative for everyone involved."
  **Tell:** H4 — Generic future-narrative closers
  **Why:** it is grammatically a prediction but contains nothing testable.
  **Fix:** `[cut]`
- **Quote:** "Together, we can achieve great things."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** a stock upbeat closer that could end any announcement.
  **Fix:** `[cut]`

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "By working together and embracing a growth mindset, we will navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale."
  **Tell:** S9 — Consultant-speak / business jargon
  **Why:** "growth mindset" and "deliver value at scale" signal work without saying what the work is, in another triplet.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: which challenges, and what value for whom]`
- **Quote:** "look forward to partnering with you as we embark on this exciting journey"
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** "embark" is a replace-on-sight word, and "journey" repeats from the previous paragraph.
  **Fix:** `look forward to working with you`
- **Quote:** "Stay tuned for more updates as we continue to unlock the full potential of our data."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** "unlock the full potential" is a vague promise, and "stay tuned" defers the content again.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: what the next update will cover, and when]`

## What already reads well
- Nothing here reads well yet — the draft is generic throughout, so there is no sentence to keep as a model.

Dear Tomas,

Our new demand forecasting approach reduced weighted MAPE across the product catalog by 3.5 percentage points, from 18.2% to 14.7%, on the last 12 weeks of data. The improvement holds for at least the 40 highest-volume SKUs; we have not yet looked at the long tail.

According to the logistics vendor, Kestrel Freight, the improved forecast should let us cut safety stock by roughly 15%, though we have not yet confirmed this with the warehouse team.

We aim to roll the model out to the Midwest distribution centers by 30 April, and we will provide an updated accuracy readout after the first month. I'm happy to discuss any of this in more detail.

Warm regards,
Keiko
items.notes: I cut the greeting filler, the "key strategic priority" framing and the "more robust, resilient supply chain" sentence, which added no fact beyond the accuracy gain. I moved "across the product catalog" onto the MAPE figure, where the scope belongs, since the next sentence says the improvement is confirmed for at least the top 40 SKUs. Numbers, the Kestrel Freight attribution, the unconfirmed safety-stock caveat, the long-tail caveat and the 30 April aim are unchanged.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.
items.notes: I made no edits. The structure and prose are already clear. Fix one conflict before you send it, because I did not pick a winner: the Summary says managers accepted schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores, but the Results section says 16 of the 23.

**Biggest problem:** The "it's not X, it's Y" construction recurs in nearly every paragraph, so the draft reads as a template with the point restated as a slogan each time.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "It's not a reporting tool, it's a decision engine."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** it sets up a contrast nobody asked for, and the next sentences already show what the platform changed.
  **Fix:** `Teams use it to make launch decisions.`
- **Quote:** "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the same construction, now as a closing aphorism that restates the theme instead of ending on a fact.
  **Fix:** `We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter.`

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "It's not about running more tests, it's about asking sharper questions."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the third use of the same setup. The sentence after it, about analysts framing hypotheses, carries the content.
  **Fix:** `Analysts now spend their time framing hypotheses with the people who own the roadmap.`
- **Quote:** "It's not a gate for launches, it's a conversation starter."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the office-hours sentence before it already shows this, so the slogan only repeats it.
  **Fix:** `[cut]`
- **Quote:** "It's not a finished product, it's a living system that improves with each experiment."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the same setup again, with a stock metaphor ("living system") in place of a plain statement.
  **Fix:** `[cut]`
- **Quote:** "Looking ahead, the platform will keep growing with the teams that use it."
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** "keep growing with the teams that use it" names no change; the concrete plan is in the next sentence.
  **Fix:** `[cut; lead with "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter."]`

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "Product managers tell us they now read experiment results before they read opinions."
  **Tell:** S4 — Vague attribution / weasel words
  **Why:** an unnamed group reports a behavior change with no count or source.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: how many product managers said this, or a named source]`
- **Quote:** "The cultural shift matters as much as the tooling."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** it says the shift matters instead of showing a consequence.
  **Fix:** `[cut; start the paragraph at the analysts sentence]`

## What already reads well
- "You might think that a stricter review step would slow teams down, but the data shows median time from proposal to launch fell from 19 days to 12 days since we introduced it." The objection is one a real reader could hold, and it is answered at once with a number, so it is evidence-backed and should stay.
- "The platform team holds weekly office hours where anyone can bring a half-formed idea and leave with a testable design." It is concrete and says who does what.

- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Finance Analytics: Planned
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Marketing Science: In progress
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Risk Modeling: In progress
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Supply Chain Analytics: Done
- Warehouse migration wave 2 cutover status for Customer Insights: Done

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes: I made no edits, since it is already clear and I read it as mostly fine. One conflict to fix before sending, because I did not pick a winner: the Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, but the Method says each arm included about 401,000.

Subject: Update on the churn early-warning model

Hi Dana,

I have some encouraging news about the churn early-warning model we have been developing. On a holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, the model surfaced at-risk subscribers with a precision of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74) among the top-decile flagged accounts. This performance holds only for postpaid customers; prepaid accounts were not evaluated, as the data was not sufficiently available.

According to the vendor, the third-party usage feed we rely on is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

This could give our retention team a way to take proactive action. Let me know if you have any questions.

Best,
Ravi
items.notes: I cut the "harnessing the power of advanced machine learning", "remarkable precision" and "game-changing" wording. I kept "encouraging" and the "could" about what the retention team might do. The precision figure, interval, postpaid-only limit, vendor attribution and two-day lag are unchanged.

items.output: Pricing test result: the $9 tier lost. Conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.6% over 21 days, with about 58,000 visitors per arm. Revenue per visitor was flat, within noise. Mobile and desktop moved together, so no segment story. I'd stop the test and keep $7. Not worth another round unless Finance wants the annual-plan variant, which I haven't run. Notebook is in the team repo if anyone wants to check my work.

**Biggest problem:** Apart from one sentence about the Atlas load test, the draft is generic enthusiasm that never says what the "modernization effort" is, so the reader cannot tell what is changing.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "This initiative represents a significant step forward in how we approach data infrastructure, and it reflects our shared commitment to excellence."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** it claims importance and "commitment to excellence" without naming a single change to the infrastructure.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: what changes in the data infrastructure, for whom, and when]`
- **Quote:** "Moving forward, we will leverage cross-functional synergies to streamline workflows and enhance the overall user experience."
  **Tell:** S9 — Consultant-speak / business jargon
  **Why:** "cross-functional synergies," "streamline workflows" and "enhance the overall user experience" name no team, workflow or user.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: which workflows change, and how]`

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "We are excited to share the next phase of our platform modernization effort."
  **Tell:** H7 — Signposting / announcements
  **Why:** it announces that news is coming instead of giving it.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: what the next phase delivers]`
- **Quote:** "By aligning around a common vision, we are positioning ourselves for long-term success."
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** "common vision" and "long-term success" are abstractions that no reader could check.
  **Fix:** `[cut]`
- **Quote:** "Our approach is holistic, scalable, and designed to meet the evolving needs of the business."
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** "holistic" is a replace-on-sight word, and the adjective list claims qualities without evidence.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: the one design choice that matters, in plain words]`
- **Quote:** "Thank you for being part of this journey. Together, we will build a stronger, more resilient data ecosystem for the future."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** a stock upbeat close ("journey," "ecosystem," "for the future") that could end any announcement.
  **Fix:** `[cut; end on the Atlas load-test result or a concrete next step]`

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "We encourage everyone to stay engaged, share feedback, and help us shape what comes next."
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** a triplet of generic calls to action with no channel or deadline.
  **Fix:** `[NEEDS: where to send feedback, and by when]`

## What already reads well
- "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms." is specific, dated and checkable. It is also stranded between generic paragraphs, so build the announcement around it and say how it relates to the modernization effort.
- "I worked really hard on this, hope it's good!" is plain and personal and matches none of the catalogued patterns, so it is not a finding. It is out of register for a team announcement, so decide whether it belongs in the piece.
